title: Economists should be worried about birth rates
gist: Noah Smith critiques a new Acemoglu-Autor-Beirne-Scott (2026) paper claiming low birth rates boost GDP-per-worker and wages via labor-saving automation, arguing the result is methodologically fragile, contradicts Acemoglu's own AI/robots research, and shouldn't be extrapolated to today's unprecedented ultra-low fertility regime — he remains worried population shrinkage is a real economic threat.

themes.theme: The Acemoglu et al. (2026) low-fertility-boosts-growth thesis

insights.claim: A 2026 paper by Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Keelan Beirne, and Andrew Scott finds that lower birth rates are associated with higher GDP-per-working-age-adult growth across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no detected negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings, which they attribute to labor-saving technology responding endogenously to scarcity of younger workers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If correct, this would materially undercut the standard bearish demographic thesis (aging = drag on growth) that underlies concerns about Japan, China, South Korea, and parts of Europe.
insights.quote: Contrary to the widespread expectation that [low birth rates] hamper economic growth, we find lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings.
insights.locator: abstract quote, early in article

insights.claim: The paper also reports that lower-birth-rate countries and US regions show more labor-saving patents, faster growth of high-tech activity, and higher total factor productivity (TFP) growth.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Would support a bull case that AI/automation adoption in aging, low-birth-rate economies (Japan, Korea, China, parts of Europe) could offset demographic drag via faster tech deployment.
insights.locator: abstract quote, early in article

insights.claim: The theoretical mechanism behind the paper — that scarce labor forces businesses to adopt labor-saving technology, which raises productivity — has historical precedent, with economic historian Robert Allen arguing this scarcity-driven mechanism is what caused the Industrial Revolution.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames a real historical model investors can use to evaluate whether tight labor markets/aging demographics push firms toward faster automation capex.
insights.locator: paragraph on 'aging, rather mechanically, creates a burden'

themes.theme: Why Smith is skeptical of the labor-scarcity-drives-innovation mechanism

insights.claim: Smith argues the labor-scarcity-boosts-innovation mechanism likely fails in the general case because people are not just labor supply but also consumers, so a smaller population means fewer consumers and thus less incentive for firms to invest in labor-saving technology.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Directly counters the bull case for 'automation offsets demographic decline' — implies shrinking-population economies may see weaker, not stronger, capex incentives for labor-saving tech.
insights.quote: Human beings aren’t just labor supply; they also create labor demand. The incentive for businesses to buy new machine tools, robots, AI, etc. is that someone is going to buy the stuff they produce with those tools.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This is actually a plausible mechanism'

insights.claim: Smith notes this is likely why empirical estimates of immigration's effect on wages are typically close to zero — new workers (like babies growing up) add both labor supply and consumer demand, roughly offsetting each other.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Useful cross-check framework: population-size shocks (immigration or birth rates) tend to be wage-neutral in aggregate because supply and demand effects offset.
insights.quote: Babies are not that different from immigrants.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This is actually a plausible mechanism'

insights.claim: A separate Acemoglu and Linn (2004) paper found that faster population growth increases pharmaceutical innovation via larger market size, which runs counter to the new paper's population-scarcity-drives-innovation thesis.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shows an internal tension in Acemoglu's own body of research on population size and innovation — worth flagging when evaluating the new paper's causal story.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This is actually a plausible mechanism'

themes.theme: Contradiction with Acemoglu's own AI and robots research

insights.claim: The new paper's core thesis — that automation raises wages in response to labor scarcity — directly contradicts Acemoglu's own prior empirical work (with Restrepo, 2017) finding that robots depress wages.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals that the 'automation solves the demographic problem' narrative rests on cherry-picked or inconsistent evidence from the same author, a red flag for anyone building an investment thesis on it.
insights.quote: Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017) find that robots depress wages, whereas the entire mechanism in Acemoglu et al. (2026) relies on automation raising wages.
insights.locator: footnote 3

insights.claim: In his 2024 paper 'The Simple Macroeconomics of AI,' Acemoglu estimates predicted TFP gains from AI over the next 10 years at less than 0.53% — a very small figure that undercuts the idea that AI-driven automation can meaningfully offset population aging.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A hard, citable number for investors modeling AI's macro productivity impact — Acemoglu himself, a leading AI-productivity skeptic, puts the 10-year TFP gain under 0.53%, far below more bullish Street/tech-industry estimates.
insights.quote: predicted TFP gains over the next 10 years [from AI] are…predicted to be less than 0.53%.
insights.locator: paragraph citing 'The Simple Macroeconomics of AI' (2024)

insights.claim: In his 2021 paper 'Harms of AI,' Acemoglu argued that if deployed on its current trajectory and left unregulated, AI could damage competition and consumer privacy, excessively automate work, fuel inequality, push down wages inefficiently, and fail to improve worker productivity.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Represents a prominent economist's downside case for unregulated AI deployment — relevant to regulatory-risk assessments for AI/automation-exposed sectors.
insights.quote: I argue that if AI continues to be deployed along its current trajectory and remains unregulated, it may produce various social, economic and political harms.
insights.locator: paragraph citing 'Harms of AI' (2021)

insights.claim: Smith argues Acemoglu cannot simultaneously claim automation will compensate for population aging via higher wages/productivity while also arguing elsewhere that automation pushes down wages without raising productivity — the two positions are logically incompatible.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A methodological caution for investors: don't take a single high-profile paper's demographic-optimism conclusion at face value when the same author's other work implies the opposite mechanism.
insights.quote: If modern automation technologies push down wages without raising productivity, it cannot compensate for population aging in the way that Acemoglu, Autor, Beirne, and Scott claim that it must — and therefore, population aging is dangerous in a way that it wasn’t before.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This stands in direct contradiction'

themes.theme: Methodological weaknesses in the paper's country-level results

insights.claim: The paper's cross-country finding that lower birth rates raise GDP per working-age adult loses statistical significance once controls for education, urbanization, and geographic region are added — and the effect weakens as more controls are added, which Smith flags as a red flag suggesting omitted-variable bias.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests the country-level result may not survive rigorous specification — investors should treat the 'low fertility boosts per-capita growth' headline finding with skepticism.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'First of all, I’m not convinced'

insights.claim: The word 'institutions' does not appear once in the new Acemoglu et al. (2026) paper, despite institutions being the centerpiece of Acemoglu's Nobel-winning body of work on economic development.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Highlights a conspicuous theoretical inconsistency — worth noting when assessing how seriously to weight the paper's causal claims about growth drivers.
insights.quote: The word “institutions” does not even appear once in this new paper!
insights.locator: paragraph on institutions/colonialism footnote

insights.claim: The paper barely analyzes GDP per capita — the metric that actually matters for living standards — despite having the data; its total-GDP result shows no correlation but with very large standard errors, meaning 'no negative impact' should be read as 'we can't detect an effect,' not as proof of no effect.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A general caution for reading any econometric paper's headline claims: 'no negative impact' framing in a noisy cross-country regression often overstates certainty, and a real positive relationship could be hiding within a wide confidence interval.
insights.quote: We shouldn’t interpret absence of evidence as evidence of absence.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Of course, what we ultimately care about'

themes.theme: Regional wage-growth result likely confounded by talent sorting

insights.claim: The paper's US commuting-zone result shows coastal cities (New York, San Francisco, Boston) had lower birth rates in 1940 and faster wage growth from 1970-2020, which the authors interpret as businesses there being forced to automate due to fewer workers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: This is the paper's strongest result (survives controls better) but is also the one Smith most directly disputes with an alternative explanation.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Anyway, the result for wages'

insights.claim: Smith argues the coastal-city wage-growth result is more plausibly explained by talent sorting and interregional mobility (skilled people moving to Boston/SF, less-skilled people moving to cheaper areas, and high-value industries like biotech, robotics, and software following the talent) than by 1940 birth-rate-driven automation, since US regions are not economically independent of each other.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the paper's Silicon Valley/coastal-tech-cluster causal story — investors should treat 'low fertility built Silicon Valley' as an unproven, contested claim rather than an established mechanism.
insights.quote: So in Acemoglu et al.’s telling, a substantial part of the reason the San Francisco Bay Area became Silicon Valley is not because the tech industry naturally tends to cluster in certain locations and draw in talented engineers and entrepreneurs, but because people in the Bay Area in 1940 didn’t have many kids... I simply don’t buy that story.
insights.locator: paragraph on Silicon Valley

insights.claim: Acemoglu and Restrepo's own 2017 research found the US commuting zones with greatest robot exposure include Detroit, Lansing, Saginaw, Defiance OH, Lorain OH, Muncie IN, Racine WI, and Wilmington DE — Rust Belt manufacturing areas, not the low-birth-rate coastal knowledge hubs the new paper's story would predict.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Cross-checkable geographic data point that undercuts the new paper's automation-follows-labor-scarcity regional narrative.
insights.locator: paragraph on Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017) commuting zones

insights.claim: Research by Enrico Moretti has shown that sorting of talent and knowledge industries was strongly correlated with income divergence between American regions after 1970, which Smith argues better explains the coastal-vs-Rust-Belt wage divergence than 1940 birth rates.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Points investors to talent-clustering/agglomeration effects (Moretti's framework) as the dominant driver of regional wage divergence over birth-rate-driven automation.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Other research — for example, by Enrico Moretti'

themes.theme: Why the past can't be extrapolated to today's ultra-low fertility

insights.claim: Economist Jesús Fernández-Villaverde argues today's fertility collapse has no historical precedent, and the seven decades of data Acemoglu et al. (2026) analyze contain nothing comparable to today's ultra-low fertility rates, making extrapolation from the historical sample dangerous.
insights.speaker: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde (quoted by Noah Smith)
insights.so_what: A core external-validity warning: any 'low fertility is fine for growth' conclusion drawn from historical (1950-2020) data should not be assumed to hold for the much lower fertility rates seen today (e.g., South Korea, China, parts of Southern/Eastern Europe).
insights.quote: The fertility collapse now underway has no historical precedent. The seven decades of data the [Acemoglu et al. (2026)] paper analyzes, however carefully, contain nothing remotely comparable to the ultra-low fertility rates we observe today…we are sailing into demographic terra incognita, and in these waters, the pretense of knowledge is the most dangerous temptation.
insights.locator: block quote from Jesús Fernández-Villaverde

insights.claim: Fernández-Villaverde calculates that a total fertility rate (TFR) of 1.56 implies each generation is 76% the size of the last (about 0.9% annual population decline, retaining ~40% of the population after 100 years), while a TFR of 0.75 implies each generation is only 37% of the last (about 3.35% annual decline, retaining only ~3.5% after a century) — roughly an 11x difference in long-run demographic outcome despite both being labeled 'low fertility.'
insights.speaker: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde (quoted by Noah Smith)
insights.so_what: Concrete quantitative framework for sizing long-run population-decline risk by country TFR — directly usable for stress-testing multi-decade demographic/GDP models for countries like South Korea (TFR near 0.75) versus more moderately low-fertility countries.
insights.quote: A TFR of 1.56 means each generation is 76% the size of the last: the population declines about 0.9% per year, so after 100 years you retain roughly 40% of the initial population. A TFR of 0.75 means each generation is 37% of the last: about a 3.35% decline per year, leaving roughly 3.5% after a century. Hence, we are dealing with a factor of about 11.
insights.locator: block quote from Jesús Fernández-Villaverde

insights.claim: A separate 2025 study by Hayashi documents a nonlinear relationship between aging and growth: countries with above-replacement fertility appear to benefit from lower birth rates, but countries already below replacement fertility appear to do worse when birth rates fall further.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Implies the growth-benefit-from-falling-fertility effect (if real) may reverse sign exactly for the countries investors are most worried about — those already below replacement (Japan, South Korea, China, Italy, etc.).
insights.locator: paragraph citing Hayashi (2025)

themes.theme: Contradicting literature and author's overall stance

insights.claim: Multiple prior studies contradict the Acemoglu et al. (2026) findings: Kremer (1993) found faster population growth led to faster technological progress; endogenous growth models (Romer 1990, Jones 2022) assume larger populations sustain faster tech progress because ideas are nonrival; Maestas, Mullen, and Powell (2023) and Ozimek, DeAntonio, and Zandi (2018) found aging was negatively correlated with productivity growth among US states from 1980-2010; and Aksoy et al. (2019) found low fertility and low population growth correlated with slower economic growth across OECD countries from 1970-2014.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A reading list of the mainstream demographic-drag-on-growth literature that the new paper's optimistic conclusion has to overcome — useful for investors weighing the credibility of the 'low fertility is fine' narrative against the weight of prior evidence.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'And it contradicts a bunch of other research'

insights.claim: Noah Smith concludes that despite Acemoglu et al. (2026) being an important contribution, it should not be regarded as definitive, and he remains personally worried about the shrinkage of the human population and believes readers should be too.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Smith's bottom-line macro view: don't treat automation as a reliable offset to demographic decline — investors modeling long-run growth for aging/shrinking economies should keep the aging-as-drag base case rather than assume tech will bail it out.
insights.quote: I’m still very worried about the shrinkage of the human race, and I think you should probably still be worried too.
insights.locator: closing paragraph

insights.claim: Smith notes the paper can be read as an implicit anti-immigration argument: if young population growth stifles automation adoption, that logically implies restricting immigration would raise wages, which would please immigration restrictionists even though it conflicts with the broader empirical literature showing immigration doesn't meaningfully lower wages.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Flags a political/policy angle: the paper's mechanism could be selectively cited to support restrictionist immigration policy, which is a policy-risk consideration for labor-intensive and immigrant-reliant sectors.
insights.quote: If young population growth stifles automation, doesn’t that mean we should restrict immigration in order to raise wages? That doesn’t mean the result is wrong, and it will certainly make MAGA types happy, but it does mean that it stands in conflict with the existing empirical literature on immigration and wages.
insights.locator: footnote 4

insights.claim: Smith argues that economics as a profession is too hierarchical and closed, with younger researchers deferring to senior authority figures and outside critics routinely dismissed, which he believes has skewed the research literature toward the priorities and intuitions of top authority figures — part of a broader 'crisis of unreliability' in academia.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A meta-lens for investors relying on academic economic research: prestige/citation count is not a reliable proxy for methodological soundness, and high-profile claims from top-cited economists deserve the same scrutiny as any other paper.
insights.quote: I believe the hierarchical, closed culture of econ has resulted in a research literature that has been too skewed toward the priorities and intuition of top authority figures.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'But for that same reason'
